statements.quote: This chapter is everything a vision model does and how it does it.

First the **mechanism** — a sliding kernel (the convolution) and the feature hierarchy it builds; then the **full pipeline** that turns features into a class; and finally the **task stack** on top — **classification → detection → segmentation → 3D** — each a harder, more spatial question than the last.

The idea of hierarchical visual feature detection was pioneered by \citeauthor{neocognitron}: he published multilayered visual feature-extraction networks as early as 1969 and introduced the \cite[Neocognitron]{neocognitron} in 1979 (English 1980), directly inspired by \citeauthorlastnameand{hubelwiesel}'s Nobel Prize–winning research on the mammalian visual cortex.
Years later, in \citeyear{lecun1989backpropagation}, LeCun et al. made the concept practical by combining convolutions with backpropagation to recognize handwritten ZIP codes for the U.S.
That 1989 system was a research prototype; the first *commercially deployed* convolutional network was the later LeNet-5, built into NCR's check-reading systems and fielded in U.S.
The prototype lineage became the mainstream in 2012.

**ImageNet** — 3.2 million images in its 2009 release (later about 14 million), organized by WordNet, with a 1,000-class ILSVRC challenge — gave vision a common benchmark of realistic difficulty (\cite[Deng et al., 2009]{deng2009imagenet}).

**AlexNet** (\cite[Krizhevsky et al., 2012]{krizhevsky2012imagenet}) trained a deep CNN on two consumer GPUs; its 7-model ensemble reached 15.3 percent top-5 error (a single model reached 18.2 percent), beating the runner-up by more than ten points.
It was not a new idea — convolutions, ReLU, and dropout all existed — but it was the demonstration, at ImageNet scale, that data and GPU compute could leave hand-engineered features behind.
The third AI boom is usually dated from that result.
\citeauthorlastnameand{hubelwiesel}'s paper serves as the direct biological blueprint for Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs):
A **convolution** is a mathematical operation that slides a small grid of numbers (the **kernel** or **filter**) across an image, computing a weighted sum at every position.

This single operation is the fundamental building block of **Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)**, the technology behind facial recognition, autonomous vehicles, medical imaging, and satellite analysis.
Where $\mathbf{I}$ is the input image, $\mathbf{K}$ is the kernel, and $(x, y)$ is the output pixel coordinate.
This is the mathematical convolution (the kernel is flipped).

Deep-learning libraries usually implement *cross-correlation* instead — the same sliding window without the flip — and for an RGB image one kernel slice per input channel is summed, not kept independent.
For a single-channel image the two operations differ only by a flip of $\mathbf{K}$.

The kernel can equally be read as a **template**: at every position the convolution measures the strength of the *match* between kernel and the patch of image beneath it — patches that resemble the kernel produce large responses, so a feature map is literally a map of where the kernel's pattern is believed to occur.
Seen this way, a convolution is a sliding search engine, and its filters are the *hypotheses* the network formed about what the image contains \cite{colah2014conv}.
In one sentence, Olah captures the whole operation:
> The kernel slides to every position of the image and computes a new pixel > as a weighted sum of the pixels it floats over.
A convolution is just “multiply the 3×3 neighbourhood by the kernel and add it up” — repeated at every position.

The Power of Hierarchy: Building Complexity from Simplicity
blocks.section: The Power of Hierarchy: Building Complexity from Simplicity

blocks.quote: A deep learning model doesn't identify a “stop sign” in a single leap. Instead, it constructs an understanding through a **layered hierarchy of abstraction**, where each successive layer examines the output of the previous one to discover increasingly complex patterns. This mirrors the architecture of the human visual cortex, where neurons in area V1 respond to simple oriented edges, while neurons in higher areas respond to faces and objects.

The first convolutional layer acts like a microscopic scanner. Each kernel examines a tiny local window of pixels (e.g., $3 \times 3$) to detect basic **primitives**: horizontal lines, vertical lines, diagonal edges, and color gradients.

At this stage, the network has no concept of a “sign”, it only knows that there is a strong vertical gradient at coordinate $(23, 41)$ or a diagonal edge at $(67, 12)$. These raw detections form **feature maps**, one per kernel.
The four feature maps below show exactly this: each filter responds to edges at a different orientation.

Beyond CNNs
ViTs: the Transformer arrives in vision
blocks.section: ViTs: the Transformer arrives in vision

blocks.quote: The **Vision Transformer (ViT)** (\cite[Dosovitskiy et al., 2021]{dosovitskiy2021vit}) splits an image into 16×16 **patches**, treats them as tokens, and runs a plain Transformer. With enough data it matches or beats the best CNNs — the convolution's inductive bias is useful but not essential. Two companions completed the picture: **MAE** (\cite[He et al., 2022]{he2021mae}), self-supervised pretraining by masking 75% of patches; and **CLIP** (\cite[Radford et al., 2021]{radford2021clip}), contrastive pretraining on (image, caption) pairs, giving vision a *text* interface — the bridge to Multimodal and Diffusion . An audit of CLIP itself then uncovered **multimodal neurons** — individual units that fire for one concept (“spider web”, a celebrity's face) whether it appears in an image or in text, foreshadowing the mechanistic-interpretability work we meet later \cite{goh2021multimodal}. A separate audit of ViTs found that the network quietly reserves a few high-norm **register** tokens as scratchpad working memory, the vision analogue of the attention sink (\cite[Darcet et al., 2024]{darcet2024registers}) (see Attention ).
blocks.section: ViTs: the Transformer arrives in vision

blocks.quote: Beyond 2D: the world

Real vision is 3D and dynamic: **pose** (keypoints), **depth**, **point clouds**, and **NeRF**-style radiance fields that render novel views. Generative models now produce 3D and video, not just stills (see Diffusion ).

To see what this perception stack *assumes* when it builds images back up, continue to [Pixels and Checkerboards](deconvolution.php) and [Inceptionism](inceptionism.php): the same filters that recognize reality are perfectly happy to hallucinate it \cite{mordvintsev2015inceptionism}.
